title: Ulyana and the Portrait
premise: Rosalind Blackwood, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards toward zero, returns to their hometown of Hollowmere when the childhood imaginary friend, Ulyana, appears on the porch unchanged after thirty years. Ulyana leads them to the town's founding secret: a well beneath the old Blackwood house that the founders sealed with a portrait ritual, feeding it memories to keep something below asleep. As the seal fails and the townspeople begin counting backwards in their sleep, Rosalind must choose between sacrificing the memory of the person they loved most or letting the well refill. In the end, Rosalind completes the founders' ritual by painting Ulyana — giving up their oldest companion — and seals the well at the cost of forgetting them entirely.
about_author: Kestrel Okafor is a former hospice volunteer from rural Ohio whose short fiction has appeared in several small-press horror anthologies. They write about grief, small towns, and the things families bury together.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. At the hospice, a dying patient counts down from one hundred and stops exactly at zero, then flatlines. Rosalind has heard this before — always at deaths they somehow predicted. The emotional beat is quiet dread: three years of rationalizations finally cracking. A letter arrives from Hollowmere: the Blackwood house has been sold, and Rosalind must sign papers or lose everything.

chapters.title: Ulyana on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Arriving in Hollowmere, Rosalind finds Ulyana waiting on the porch — the imaginary friend from age six, unchanged, while Rosalind has aged. Ulyana speaks in riddles about 'the water rising.' The beat is uncanny tenderness mixed with terror; Rosalind, starved for connection, wants to believe despite every instinct. Neighbors watch the house but won't come near it.

chapters.title: What the Founders Buried
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Searching the attic, Rosalind finds the founders' ledger: four families, including the Blackwoods, sealed something in a well beneath the house using a ritual called the Portrait — each founder painted a beloved memory into an image and burned it. One portrait was never completed. Ulyana grows agitated whenever Rosalind touches the ledger. Beat: dread deepening into compulsion.

chapters.title: The Town That Sleeps Wrong
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In town, everyone is polite and hollow-eyed; children draw the same spiral well in crayon. At the diner, an old woman whispers that the Blackwoods were supposed to keep the watch, and asks if Rosalind can still hear the counting. That night, Rosalind dreams of descending stairs behind the pantry wall. Beat: isolation — the town knows more than it says.

chapters.title: Behind the Pantry
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Rosalind breaks through the false pantry wall and finds the stone stairwell, the well mouth breathing cold air upward, and three finished portraits nailed around it like sentinels. Ulyana refuses to follow them down. When Rosalind leans over the edge, they hear hundreds of voices counting backward in unison. Beat: awe curdling into horror; the rationalizations are dead now.

chapters.title: The Fourth Portrait
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Researching the ledger, Rosalind learns their grandmother was the fourth founder who fled before finishing her portrait — which is why the seal weakens generationally. The unfinished canvas hangs in the attic, blank except for a faint outline of a child. Ulyana admits, finally, what they are: a memory given form, the grandmother's unfinished offering. Beat: betrayal and pity entwined.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: POV alternating Rosalind and townsfolk via letters. The well begins refilling: pets vanish, the diner woman dies mid-count, and Rosalind starts hearing the countdown in their own head at night. Ulyana begs Rosalind to leave Hollowmere forever. The beat is desperation — love against duty made literal, as staying means becoming part of the ritual.

chapters.title: What I Would Burn
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Rosalind prepares the ritual, learning the price: the painter must give up the memory they love most, rendered truly enough to hold the thing below. For Rosalind, that memory is Ulyana themselves — the one constant love of their life. Ulyana, understanding, quietly helps mix the paints. Beat: devastating acceptance; duty and love converge on the same sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Ritual of Portraits
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. As the well breaches and the counting becomes a roar through the whole town, Rosalind paints Ulyana from memory — every detail, every kindness — and carries the canvas down the stairwell as the thing below reaches for them. They nail the fourth portrait beside its sisters and speak the founders' words. Beat: climax; terror transfigured into devotion.

chapters.title: The Nurse Who Forgot
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind, fragmented. Weeks later, Rosalind signs the sale papers and leaves Hollowmere, feeling a grief they cannot name, a shape missing from every memory. Back at the hospice, a dying patient counts down — and this time Rosalind hears nothing at all. On the windowsill sits a child's drawing of two friends holding hands. Final beat: bittersweet resolution; the cost of sealing the dark is losing the light you used to see it by.
